sections.h2: Billing and paying in Madison County
sections.html:
Property tax here goes through a Treasurer in Edwardsville, who bills in four installments. Due dates fall in July, September, October and December, on the 9th of each month, and bills go out in early June. Look for those months on your own bill.

The Treasurer's counter is in the Madison County Administration Building, 157 N. Main Street, Suite 125, Edwardsville, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Other ways to pay: online by e-check or card, by mailed check, or at one of nearly 100 collector banks and credit unions around the county, which require the bill coupon. Mail with the coupon goes to P.O. Box 849, and mail without it to P.O. Box 729, both in Edwardsville 62025. Cards add a 2.5 percent charge that goes to the card companies, and each transaction must be at least $2.50.

Partial online payments are not offered. To pay part of an installment, go to the office. Only an account holder can schedule all four installments in advance.

sections.h2: Late payment and the tax sale
sections.html:
Illinois law adds a 1.5 percent penalty every 30 days on the unpaid balance of a late installment. It starts one day after the deadline and runs until the installment is paid or the tax is sold. What follows:

  • A delinquency notice goes out by certified mail about a month before the annual tax sale, and a $10 certified fee is added to the bill.
  • Delinquent parcel numbers, owners and amounts are printed in a local newspaper.
  • Unpaid taxes are sold at the annual tax sale, and the owner can redeem for two to three years.
  • After the sale, the County Clerk mails a take notice for the tax buyer. Penalties bid at the sale run from 18 percent down to 0 percent, because bidding starts high and falls.
  • About two years after the sale, the Circuit Clerk and Sheriff tell the owner the buyer plans to ask the court for a tax deed. At about two and a half years, the buyer can petition for the deed.

Redemptions go through the Madison County Clerk and require the full amount owed, in cash, money order or cashier's check. Not receiving a bill is no defense, since 35 ILCS 200/20-15 says a failure to mail or receive a bill does not affect the tax. Call the Treasurer at (618) 692-6260 for a duplicate.

Your township assessor, elected to a four-year term, inspects, lists and values each property, and the Chief County Assessment Office reviews those numbers. Assessed value is one-third of fair market value, so dividing the assessed value by .3333 shows the market value the office is using.

Before you file anything, the county suggests an informal talk with the assessor sometime from New Year's Day through the end of May in the assessment year.

If the informal talk does not settle it, file a formal complaint with the Board of Review, a three-member panel appointed by the County Board. The complaint session opens the day the Chief County Assessment Officer publishes assessment changes, and the window then stays open for 30 days. Only the Board's own forms are processed, with separate forms for residential, commercial and farm property, and an LLC must use an attorney. Mail forms to the Madison County Board of Review, 157 N. Main St., Suite 222, Edwardsville, IL 62025.

There are three grounds for an appeal:

  1. A fact on your property record card is wrong, such as the bath count or square footage.
  2. The estimated market value is too high, shown by recent sales or a purchase price below the assessed figure.
  3. The value may be accurate but is inequitable because similar homes are assessed lower.

The comparable grid asks for three similar properties. For an equity case, divide the improvement assessment by square footage for each home and compare. A complaint that taxes are too high will not win, because assessment officials set values, not taxes. Beyond the Board sits the five-member Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board.

Once the tax bill is out, it is too late to appeal that year's assessment. The assessment office finalizes values around the end of each year, certifies them to the state and passes them to the County Clerk, which closes the file. The one exception is a calculation error on the bill itself, such as an exemption that was never applied. Contact the assessment office if you spot one.

You can also pay under protest and file a tax objection complaint in circuit court, though a protest without a prior Board of Review appeal rarely goes well. Madison County is not covered by the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law that caps yearly increases in other counties.

About 220 taxing districts each adopt their own levy. Your bill multiplies the total rate per $100 of taxable assessed value by that value, then adds special assessments such as a drainage and levee district charge, which lands in the first installment.

Several exemptions reduce the equalized assessed value before the rate is applied:

You cannot freeze your taxes outright, but an owner 65 or older who lives in the home and has household income of $75,000 or less can apply for the Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze Homestead Exemption. Check your bill for these lines before you list a house. A missing exemption is a billing error you can fix.

Madison is part of the Metro East beside St. Louis and the largest county in southern Illinois, with 263,110 residents (July 2025) and 119,947 housing units. Owner-occupancy is 74.2 percent, median owner-occupied value is $173,000, median household income is $75,793, and typical monthly rent is $1,024. Builders took out 435 permits in 2025. Edwardsville is the seat and Granite City is the largest city.

School districts include Edwardsville CUSD 7, Alton CUSD 11, Collinsville CUSD 10, Granite City CUSD 9 and Highland CUSD 5. Rates differ sharply by district, so compare the taxing bodies on your bill with those a buyer will see next door.

sections.h2: Selling with a Madison County tax bill
sections.html: Installments come due in July, September, October and December, so a closing between dates can leave a partly paid year. Ask the Treasurer what is paid and what is open, and have the title company prorate the rest. If an older year went unpaid, get the County Clerk's redemption amount before you set a price. A cash buyer can close on those figures without waiting for a lender.

faqs.q: When are Madison County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Four installments, due in July, September, October and December, on the 9th of each month. Mobile home tax is a separate single payment.

faqs.q: Does Madison County charge interest on late installments?
faqs.a: A 1.5 percent penalty applies to each late installment every 30 days after its due date. Unpaid taxes are eventually sold at the annual tax sale, and the owner can redeem for two to three years through the County Clerk.

faqs.q: What is the Madison County appeal deadline?
faqs.a: The Board of Review filing window stays open for 30 days from the day the Chief County Assessment Officer publishes assessment changes. After the tax bill comes out, that year's assessment can no longer be changed.

faqs.q: Who do I call with a question about my Madison County tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Treasurer at (618) 692-6260 for payments and duplicate bills. For assessment or exemption problems, contact your township assessor or the Chief County Assessment Office.

faqs.q: Does Madison County cap how much taxes can rise?
faqs.a: No. The Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, which limits annual increases in other Illinois counties, does not apply here. Taxing districts set their own levies each year.
